METABRIC Breast Cancer Analysis¶

Part 2: Bayesian Logistic Regression¶

Author: Angela Holm
Project Focus: Breast Cancer Biomarkers, Age at Diagnosis, and Overall Survival
Dataset: METABRIC Breast Cancer Clinical Dataset
Tools: Python, Pandas, NumPy, PyMC, ArviZ, Matplotlib, SciPy, Jupyter Notebook

Project Overview¶

Part 2 builds on the exploratory data analysis completed in Part 1 by using Bayesian logistic regression to examine the relationships between age at diagnosis, estrogen receptor (ER) status, progesterone receptor (PR) status, HER2 status, and recorded overall survival.

The analysis uses clinical data from the Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC) study. Bayesian modeling will be used to estimate the associations between these clinical characteristics and recorded mortality while accounting for uncertainty in the results.

Research Question¶

How are age at diagnosis, ER status, PR status, and HER2 status associated with overall survival status among patients diagnosed with breast cancer?

Analytical Approach¶

The analysis will prepare the clinical variables for modeling, define a Bayesian logistic regression model using PyMC, and evaluate the resulting posterior distributions. Model diagnostics, credible intervals, and odds ratios will be used to interpret the associations between the selected predictors and recorded mortality.

The findings will be interpreted as statistical associations rather than evidence of causation.

1. Data Preparation and Cleaning for Bayesian Logistic Regression¶

Before developing the Bayesian logistic regression model, the METABRIC clinical dataset was reviewed and prepared to ensure that the selected variables were complete and appropriately formatted. The original dataset contains 500 patient records and 39 clinical variables. The analysis focuses on age at diagnosis, estrogen receptor (ER) status, progesterone receptor (PR) status, HER2 status, and recorded overall survival status.

Variable Selection¶

Five variables were selected for the Bayesian model:

  • ER_STATUS — Estrogen receptor classification.
  • PR_STATUS — Progesterone receptor classification.
  • HER2_STATUS — HER2 classification.
  • AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS — Patient age at breast cancer diagnosis.
  • OS_STATUS — Recorded overall survival status.

ER, PR, HER2, and age at diagnosis serve as the predictor variables, while overall survival status is the binary outcome. These variables were selected to examine how patient age and clinical biomarker classifications are associated with recorded mortality when evaluated together.

Missing-Value Assessment and Cleaning¶

The five selected variables were examined for missing values and data types before modeling. ER status and age at diagnosis contained 500 non-missing observations, while PR status, HER2 status, and overall survival status each contained 496 non-missing observations.

Observations with missing values in any of the five selected variables were removed using Pandas dropna(). This reduced the dataset from 500 to 496 complete patient records, representing the removal of four observations (0.8%).

A subsequent verification confirmed that no missing values remained in the selected variables. The resulting dataset was retained for the Bayesian logistic regression analysis.

Encoding Categorical Variables¶

The clinical biomarker classifications and survival outcome were converted into binary numerical variables to make them suitable for Bayesian logistic regression.

The following coding was applied:

  • ER: Negative = 0, Positive = 1
  • PR: Negative = 0, Positive = 1
  • HER2: Negative = 0, Positive = 1
  • Mortality: Living = 0, Deceased = 1

The encoded variables were reviewed to confirm that the classifications were correctly represented. The final dataset contained 384 ER-positive and 112 ER-negative patients, 252 PR-positive and 244 PR-negative patients, and 52 HER2-positive and 444 HER2-negative patients.

This encoding allows the Bayesian model to estimate differences in the log-odds of recorded mortality between biomarker-positive and biomarker-negative patients while accounting for the other included predictors.

Standardization of Age at Diagnosis¶

Age at diagnosis was standardized before being included in the Bayesian model. Unlike the biomarker classifications, age is a continuous numerical variable measured in years.

Standardization was performed by subtracting the mean age from each observation and dividing by the standard deviation. This created a new variable, AGE_STD, with a mean approximately equal to zero and a standard deviation of one.

Standardizing age places it on a consistent scale and can improve the efficiency of Bayesian sampling. It also means that the model's age coefficient represents the change in log-odds of recorded mortality associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in age at diagnosis.

The standardized values were verified before proceeding with model development.

Preparation for Bayesian Modeling¶

Following cleaning and transformation, the dataset contained 496 complete patient records, three binary biomarker predictors, one standardized age predictor, and a binary mortality outcome.

These variables provide the inputs for the Bayesian logistic regression model developed in the next section. The model will estimate posterior distributions for the relationships between age, biomarker classifications, and recorded mortality while accounting for uncertainty in the estimated coefficients.

Because overall survival status is treated as a binary outcome, the analysis evaluates associations with recorded mortality rather than time-to-event survival or causal relationships.

2. Bayesian Logistic Regression Model Development¶

Model Construction and Prior Distributions¶

A Bayesian logistic regression model was developed using PyMC to examine the relationships between breast cancer biomarker classifications, age at diagnosis, and recorded mortality in the METABRIC dataset. The model included 496 patients with complete clinical information.

The dependent variable was mortality, coded as 0 for living patients and 1 for deceased patients. ER, PR, and HER2 were included as binary predictors, while age at diagnosis was standardized before modeling.

The model included an intercept and four regression coefficients. Normal prior distributions with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 5 were assigned to all five parameters. These priors allow for a range of possible relationships while expressing no initial preference for positive or negative coefficients.

A logistic transformation was applied to the linear combination of predictors to estimate the probability of recorded mortality. A Bernoulli likelihood was then used because the dependent variable has two possible outcomes.

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Sampling¶

Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling was performed using PyMC's No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) to estimate the posterior distributions of the regression coefficients.

The sampling procedure used four independent chains, with 1,000 tuning iterations and 2,000 posterior draws per chain. This produced 8,000 posterior draws after tuning. A target acceptance rate of 0.90 was specified, and a random seed of 42 was used to support reproducibility.

Rather than producing only one coefficient estimate for each predictor, Bayesian sampling generates a distribution of plausible parameter values based on the observed clinical data and the specified prior distributions.

These posterior distributions provide the basis for evaluating the direction, magnitude, and uncertainty of the relationships between the selected clinical variables and recorded mortality.

In [13]:
# Define the Bayesian logistic regression model

with pm.Model() as logistic_model:

    # Priors
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta_ER = pm.Normal("beta_ER", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta_PR = pm.Normal("beta_PR", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta_HER2 = pm.Normal("beta_HER2", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta_Age = pm.Normal("beta_Age", mu=0, sigma=5)

    # Linear predictor
    eta = (
        beta0
        + beta_ER * model_clean["ER"].values
        + beta_PR * model_clean["PR"].values
        + beta_HER2 * model_clean["HER2"].values
        + beta_Age * model_clean["AGE_STD"].values
    )

    # Logistic transformation
    p = pm.math.sigmoid(eta)

    # Likelihood
    mortality = pm.Bernoulli(
        "mortality",
        p=p,
        observed=model_clean["Mortality"].values
    )
In [14]:
# Run MCMC sampling using the No-U-Turn Sampler

with logistic_model:
    trace = pm.sample(
        draws=2000,
        tune=1000,
        chains=4,
        cores=4,
        target_accept=0.90,
        random_seed=42,
        return_inferencedata=True
    )

3. Posterior Analysis and Model Diagnostics¶
Posterior Distribution Summary¶
Following MCMC sampling, the posterior distributions were summarized using ArviZ. The summary included the posterior mean, standard deviation, 95% highest density interval (HDI), Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE), effective sample size (ESS), and R-hat convergence statistic for each regression coefficient.


The 95% HDI represents an interval containing 95% of the posterior probability for a parameter. These intervals help evaluate the direction and uncertainty of the estimated relationships. When an HDI includes zero, the posterior distribution remains compatible with both positive and negative coefficient values within that interval.


Trace Plots and Convergence Diagnostics¶
Trace plots were generated for the intercept and four predictor coefficients to examine the behavior of the MCMC chains. These plots display the sampled parameter values across iterations alongside their posterior distributions.


The trace plots were used to assess whether the chains mixed adequately and explored similar regions of the posterior distributions. Additional convergence checks were performed using R-hat and effective sample size statistics.


All five parameters had R-hat values of 1.00, indicating no apparent convergence problems based on this diagnostic. The bulk effective sample sizes ranged from 5,241 to 6,570, while the tail effective sample sizes ranged from 4,895 to 5,491. These results indicate that the posterior estimates were supported by substantial effective sample sizes.


Posterior Predictive Checks¶
Posterior predictive sampling was also performed to examine how well the fitted Bayesian model could reproduce the observed mortality outcomes.


Using the posterior distributions, PyMC generated simulated mortality observations, which were compared with the observed data using ArviZ posterior predictive plots. This provides an additional assessment of model fit beyond examining the regression coefficients and MCMC convergence statistics.


Because mortality is a binary outcome, the posterior predictive comparison focuses on whether the model can reproduce the overall distribution of living and deceased patients. It does not, by itself, establish how accurately the model predicts individual patient outcomes.


Together, these diagnostic procedures provide information about sampling reliability, posterior uncertainty, and the model's ability to represent the observed data.

4. Results and Interpretation¶
Bayesian Logistic Regression Results¶
The Bayesian logistic regression model examined the relationships between ER status, PR status, HER2 status, age at diagnosis, and recorded mortality among 496 patients in the METABRIC dataset. Of these patients, 288 (58.1%) were living and 208 (41.9%) were deceased.


The posterior results showed differences in both the direction and uncertainty of the estimated relationships.


Age at Diagnosis


Age at diagnosis demonstrated the strongest positive association with recorded mortality among the standardized and binary predictors included in the model. The posterior mean coefficient was 0.991, with a 95% HDI ranging from 0.766 to 1.215.


Because the entire interval was above zero, the posterior results support a positive association between increasing age at diagnosis and the odds of recorded mortality, after accounting for ER, PR, and HER2 status.


Estrogen Receptor (ER) Status


ER-positive status had a negative posterior mean coefficient of -0.508, with a 95% HDI ranging from -1.070 to 0.053.


The negative coefficient suggests that ER-positive patients may have lower odds of recorded mortality compared with ER-negative patients when the other predictors are held constant. However, because the 95% HDI includes zero, uncertainty remains about the direction and magnitude of this relationship.


Progesterone Receptor (PR) Status


PR-positive status also showed a negative posterior mean coefficient of -0.212, with a 95% HDI ranging from -0.697 to 0.260.


Although the posterior mean suggests a possible association with lower mortality odds, the interval includes zero and extends into positive values. The findings therefore do not provide strong evidence of a consistent relationship between PR status and recorded mortality after accounting for the other predictors.


HER2 Status


HER2-positive status demonstrated a positive posterior mean coefficient of 0.721, with a 95% HDI ranging from 0.028 to 1.415.


The entire 95% HDI was above zero, supporting a positive association between HER2-positive status and the odds of recorded mortality. However, the interval was relatively wide, indicating uncertainty about the magnitude of this relationship.


Model Convergence and Reliability¶
The MCMC sampling procedure produced 8,000 posterior draws across four chains following tuning. All five model parameters had R-hat values of 1.00, with bulk and tail effective sample sizes exceeding 4,800.


These diagnostics support the reliability of the posterior sampling results, although convergence alone does not establish that the statistical model fully represents the underlying clinical relationships.


Posterior predictive sampling was also performed to compare simulated mortality outcomes with the observed data. This provided an additional method for evaluating how well the fitted model reproduced the distribution of the binary outcome.


Overall Interpretation¶
The Bayesian analysis identified age at diagnosis and HER2-positive status as predictors with positive posterior associations with recorded mortality. ER-positive and PR-positive status had negative posterior mean coefficients, but their 95% HDIs included zero, indicating greater uncertainty about these relationships.


These findings suggest that patient age and biomarker classification may contribute differently to recorded mortality outcomes. The Bayesian approach was particularly useful because it provided posterior distributions and credible intervals rather than relying exclusively on individual coefficient estimates.


However, the analysis has important limitations. The model uses overall survival status as a binary outcome without accounting for differences in follow-up time, treatment, disease stage, or other clinical factors. Consequently, the findings should be interpreted as associations with recorded mortality rather than estimates of time-to-event survival or evidence of causation.


Overall, the results demonstrate how Bayesian logistic regression can be used to examine clinical relationships while explicitly representing uncertainty in the estimated effects.
